title: Invert Binary Tree
directAnswer: Mirror the tree: at every node, swap its left and right children. The recursive answer is four lines — swap the two child pointers, then recurse into both subtrees (order doesn't matter). The iterative answer does the same swap while walking the tree with a queue (BFS) or stack (DFS). Both are O(n) time, O(h) space. This is the famous problem Max Howell reportedly bombed at a Google interview.

remember.pattern: Recursive mirror — swap children at every node
remember.formula:
invert(node):
    if node is null: return null
    node.left, node.right = invert(node.right), invert(node.left)
    return node
rules: The whole problem is one operation: **swap left and right** at every node.
Recurse *and* swap — visiting without swapping does nothing; swapping only the root mirrors one level.
In Java you need a **temp variable** to swap; in Python use tuple unpacking and you can swap and recurse in one line.
Order of the two recursive calls is irrelevant — each subtree's inversion is independent.
Iterative BFS/DFS works identically: pop a node, swap its children, push both children.
whenToUse: You must produce the mirror image of a tree
Any per-node structural transformation that recurses into both subtrees
Warm-up to confirm you can write a clean recursive tree mutation
antiSignals: You must compare two trees, not transform one → Same Tree / Symmetric Tree
Only values change, not structure → a plain traversal suffices
The tree is a BST and order must be preserved → inverting destroys the BST property
remember.takeaway: Invert Binary Tree is the canonical 'recurse into both children and do one thing per node' problem. The 'one thing' here is swapping the two child pointers. Master the shape and you have the template for half of all easy tree questions.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can translate 'mirror the tree' into a clean recursive mutation that both swaps children and recurses, and whether you can produce an iterative equivalent on request.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Swapping the children but forgetting to recurse (only the top level mirrors), or recursing but forgetting to actually swap (nothing changes).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Note that the recursion order is irrelevant, show the one-line Python tuple swap, and offer the iterative BFS/DFS version to demonstrate you understand recursion is interchangeable with an explicit queue/stack.

problemStatement:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, **invert** the tree, and return its root.

Inverting means producing the mirror image: for every node, its left and right subtrees are swapped.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 100]
An empty tree inverts to an empty tree
understanding: Transform the tree in place (or rebuild it) so it becomes its own mirror image. Every node keeps its value; only the left/right child pointers are swapped, all the way down. Return the same root.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should I mutate the input tree in place or return a new tree?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: In place is standard and expected here — we swap pointers and return the same root. Mention you could clone first if the caller must keep the original.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the tree be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — node count can be 0. The null base case handles it: inverting an empty tree returns null.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the order of recursive calls matter?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Inverting the left subtree and inverting the right subtree are independent, so either order yields the same result.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Recursive or iterative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Lead with recursive (cleanest). Offer the iterative BFS (queue) or DFS (stack) version since it's a natural follow-up and avoids deep call stacks.

examples.explanation: Every node's children swap: under 4, the 2 and 7 subtrees switch sides; under each, their children switch too.
The root keeps value 2; its children 1 and 3 swap places.
An empty tree is its own mirror — nothing to swap.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Recursion is the cleanest; the iterative queue/stack version is the same swap with an explicit container.

approaches.name: Recursive DFS — Swap and Recurse (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Start here. It's the cleanest possible solution and shows you grasp the recursive structure immediately.
hints: What single operation, applied at every node, turns a tree into its mirror image?
At each node, swap its left and right child pointers. Then you still need to mirror the contents of each subtree — how do you reach them?
Swap the children, then recurse into both subtrees (order doesn't matter). Base case: a null node returns null.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each of the n nodes is visited once and does an O(1) pointer swap → O(n) time. Recursion depth equals the height h → O(h) space, ranging from O(log n) balanced to O(n) for a skewed tree.
approaches.explanation:
Inverting a tree is the same simple action repeated everywhere: at each node, exchange its two children. Do that at every node and the whole tree becomes its mirror.

**The recursive structure.** Handle the null node first (an empty subtree inverts to nothing). For a real node, swap `node.left` and `node.right`, then recursively invert both subtrees. That's it — the recursion guarantees the swap reaches every level, and the per-node swap guarantees each level is mirrored.

**Why the order of the two recursive calls doesn't matter.** Inverting the left subtree and inverting the right subtree touch disjoint sets of nodes, so they're fully independent. You can swap first then recurse, or recurse first then swap, or recurse left before right or right before left — every combination produces the identical mirrored tree. This is a nice point to state out loud because it shows you reason about *independence* rather than just pattern-matching code.

**Java vs Python swap.** Java has no tuple unpacking, so you stash one child in a `temp` variable before overwriting. Python lets you write `node.left, node.right = node.right, node.left` — and you can even fold the recursion into the same line: `node.left, node.right = invert(node.right), invert(node.left)`. Both are correct; the Python one-liner is a small flourish worth knowing.

**The lore.** This is the problem behind the famous tweet — Homebrew's creator was reportedly rejected by Google for being unable to invert a binary tree on a whiteboard. The takeaway for you: it's genuinely easy, but only if you've internalized the swap-and-recurse template, so don't let nerves turn four lines into a struggle.
approaches.insight: Two things must both happen at every node: the swap (which mirrors this level) and the recursion (which carries the swap downward). Drop either and you get a no-op or a one-level flip. Saying 'swap AND recurse, both required' out loud is the quickest way to prove you understand why it works.

dryRun.intro: We swap children top-down. Each line shows a node after its children are swapped (recursion then fixes the subtrees).

steps.action: no children to swap → return as-is

code.python:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def invertTree(self, root: TreeNode) -> TreeNode:
    if not root:                         # base case
        return None
    # swap children AND recurse, all in one line via tuple unpacking
    root.left, root.right = self.invertTree(root.right), self.invertTree(root.left)
    return root

java.explanation: Base case — an empty subtree has nothing to invert.
Java needs a temp to swap, otherwise you'd overwrite left before reading it.
Right child moves to the left slot.
The stashed original left moves to the right slot — swap complete.
Recurse to mirror the (now-swapped) subtrees; order vs root.right doesn't matter.

python.explanation: Base case — None inverts to None.
RHS is fully evaluated first, so both recursive inversions happen, then the results are assigned swapped.
Return the same root — the tree was mutated in place.

No children to swap; both recursive calls hit null → returns the node unchanged.

pitfalls: Recursing without swapping (or swapping without recursing) — one mirrors nothing, the other mirrors only the root.
In Java, assigning root.left = root.right before saving the old left — you lose the left subtree.

approaches.name: Iterative BFS/DFS — Swap with a Queue or Stack
approaches.whenToMention: Offer when asked for an iterative version or when the tree could be deep enough to overflow the recursion stack.
hints: Recursion just uses a hidden stack. What explicit container could you use to visit every node and swap its children?
Push the root into a queue (BFS) or stack (DFS). Repeatedly pop a node, swap its two children, then push the non-null children.
It doesn't matter whether you swap before or after pushing the children, as long as you push whatever ends up in the left/right slots so they get processed too.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is enqueued/pushed and processed exactly once with an O(1) swap → O(n) time. A BFS queue can hold up to the tree's maximum width (O(n) in the worst level); a DFS stack holds up to O(h). Worst-case extra space is O(n).
approaches.explanation:
The iterative version makes the traversal container explicit instead of relying on the call stack. The per-node work is identical: swap the node's two children.

**BFS with a queue.** Seed a queue with the root. While the queue is non-empty, dequeue a node, swap its `left` and `right`, and enqueue both children if they exist. This processes the tree level by level, mirroring each node as it's visited.

**DFS with a stack.** Identical, but use a stack (LIFO) instead of a queue (FIFO). The traversal order differs, but since every node gets swapped exactly once and the swaps are independent, the final mirrored tree is the same.

**Why pick this over recursion.** Two reasons to mention: (1) the recursion depth on a degenerate (linked-list-shaped) tree could be O(n) and overflow the call stack in languages with small stack limits, and (2) some interviewers explicitly ask 'can you do it without recursion?' to confirm you understand recursion is just a managed stack. Functionally the two solutions are equivalent in time and asymptotic space.
approaches.insight: Recursion and an explicit stack are interchangeable; swapping a queue for that stack just changes the visiting order from depth-first to breadth-first. Since the swap at each node is independent of every other, the *order* you visit nodes never affects the result — only whether you visit them all.

python.explanation: deque gives O(1) popleft for an efficient queue.
BFS order — change to pop() for a DFS stack instead.
Only enqueue real children to avoid pushing None.

edgeCases.behavior: Guard returns null before the queue is touched.
Queue peaks at ~n/2 nodes (the last level) → O(n) space, the BFS worst case.
Queue holds at most 1-2 nodes at a time → effectively O(1) extra space for BFS here, vs O(n) recursion depth for DFS.

pitfalls: Enqueuing null children — clutters the queue and can cause null dereferences depending on the guard.
Forgetting the empty-tree guard before seeding the queue.
Assuming BFS and DFS give different trees — they don't; only the visiting order differs.

commonMistakes: Swapping children but forgetting to recurse — only the root level gets mirrored.
Recursing but forgetting to swap — the tree is unchanged.
In Java, overwriting root.left before saving it, losing the left subtree.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Swap without recursion (only one level flips)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Swapping just the root's two children mirrors a single level. Without recursing, every deeper level keeps its original orientation.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Java swap without a temp variable
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Assigning root.left = root.right first overwrites the left pointer, so the subsequent root.right = root.left just copies the right subtree onto both sides — the original left subtree is lost.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
root.left = root.right;   // original left is now unreachable
root.right = root.left;   // copies right onto right — both subtrees identical

followupVariations.title: Symmetric Tree
followupVariations.hint: Don't invert — instead check whether the tree is a mirror of itself by comparing left and right subtrees in mirror order.

followupVariations.title: Same Tree
followupVariations.hint: Parallel DFS comparing two trees node-by-node — the comparison cousin of this transformation.

followupVariations.title: Flip Equivalent Binary Trees
followupVariations.hint: Two trees are flip-equivalent if a series of these child swaps makes them identical.

followupVariations.title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
followupVariations.hint: Same recurse-into-both-children skeleton, aggregating heights instead of swapping.

patternNote: Per-node structural mutation via DFS: do one O(1) operation at every node and recurse into both children. Here the operation is a child swap. The same skeleton (recurse both sides, do one thing per node) drives Maximum Depth, Same Tree, and most easy tree problems.
